title: Meant for good (Genesis 50:15–21)
hookLine: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good
carry: fear not, I will nourish you

cards: Seventeen years in Egypt. Then Jacob dies with his sons around him, and they carry his body home to Canaan, to be buried with Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah. A huge funeral procession, Egyptians and all.
And on the way back, the brothers start doing math. Dad's gone. Dad was the reason Joseph was kind to us.
What if he's been waiting? So they send Joseph a message: before he died, your father told us to tell you, please forgive your brothers. Genesis never records Jacob saying it.
Readers have wondered ever since if the brothers made it up.

teach.h: AM I IN THE PLACE OF GOD?
teach.b: When Joseph hears it, he weeps. Seventeen years of kindness, and they still think he's waiting to strike. The brothers fall down before him one more time: we are your servants.
And Joseph says, in the King James Bible: "Fear not: for am I in the place of God?" Revenge isn't his job.

teach.h: YE THOUGHT EVIL; GOD MEANT GOOD.
teach.b: Then the sentence the whole Joseph story has been building to: "But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive."
It doesn't say the brothers meant well. It doesn't say the pit was good, or the slavery, or the prison. It says two things were happening in the same events.
They meant evil. God meant good.

This is what Christians call providence, from the Latin providentia, foresight: the belief that God is at work through history, even through human wrongdoing, toward good. Christians hold it in different ways.
Some traditions, many Reformed churches among them, stress that God governs all things, even the hard ones. Others prefer to say God permits evil without willing it, and works good out of it.
Joseph's sentence leaves room for both. Paul says something close in Romans: all things work together for good to them that love God.
And Joseph ends with care, not theology: fear not, I will nourish you and your little ones.
And he comforted them, and spoke kindly to them.

how: Christians often turn to Genesis 50:20 and Romans 8:28 in times of loss or injustice, and the doctrine of providence is taught in catechisms and confessions across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches, in differing forms.

o: a reward God gives to people who do right
God at work through history, even wrongs, toward good
the belief that everything that happens is good

games.q: what's inside the ending — tap the pairs.
p: am I in the place of God?

s: Joseph says the brothers really meant well
"ye thought evil against me." he names it, then says God meant it for good.
Genesis records Jacob asking Joseph to forgive his brothers
only the brothers report it; the text never shows Jacob saying it.
Joseph wept when he heard the brothers' message
after seventeen years, they still feared his revenge.

games.q: you're Joseph. your father is dead. your brothers fall down before you, afraid you'll finally pay them back. what do you do?
o: make them serve you, as the dreams said.
say: am I in the place of God? you meant evil, God meant good.
send them back to Canaan without grain.
games.why: "Fear not: for am I in the place of God?" then he promises to provide for them and their little ones, and speaks kindly to them.

practice: Pick something from your past that hurt, not the worst thing, something you've had time to live past.

Don't pretend it was good; look gently at what came after, a friendship, a strength, a kindness you now know how to give, and let both be true. If you pray, you can give thanks for what grew; if you don't, simply notice it.

wordCard.voice: Providence. From the Latin for foresight: the belief that God is at work through all of history, even through wrongs people do, toward good.

orig.note: Latin: foresight, from providere, to see ahead. the word Christians later used for God's care over all things.

carryVoice: Your line: fear not, I will nourish you. Not revenge: bread for the little ones. Day three hundred seventy-five.
